context: process factory · spray dryer, presses, glazing lines and roller kiln; one supplier's line governs

brief.intro: New to this project type? A tile factory turns clay and minerals into ceramic tiles in a continuous line. Raw materials are ground wet in large ball mills, the slurry is dried into a fine powder in a tall spray-dryer tower, hydraulic presses form the tiles, a dryer removes moisture, the tiles are glazed and digitally printed, and a long roller kiln fires them in under an hour. Sorting and packing machines finish the job. Almost all of this equipment comes from one or two specialist suppliers who also supervise installation, so their delivery and their technicians set the pace. The spray dryer and the kiln are the tall and the long items around which the building is arranged, and the start-up of the kiln on gas is the key commissioning event.

must_get_right: Choose the line supplier and freeze the layout first — building dimensions, foundations and the spray-dryer height all come from the supplier's drawings.
The spray-dryer tower and the kiln line fix the building: the tower may need a higher bay or to stand outside, and the kiln needs an uninterrupted straight run.
Gas supply at the required pressure is essential for the spray dryer and the kiln — a late gas connection stops commissioning entirely.
Supplier technicians install and start up in a fixed order; align the civil and steel handover dates of each area with their arrival.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by plant area along the process line and by discipline, with every long-lead machine tracked from order to factory test, shipping and arrival.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar for construction; equipment installation may run extended shifts under vendor supervision. Commissioning follows the vendor's programme, and hot commissioning runs continuously once started.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Supplier drawings → foundations (mill bases, press pits, kiln floor, tower) → building → floor → installation area by area in process order → gas, power, air and water → cold tests → spray dryer and kiln heat-up → first tiles → tuning. The critical path runs through the line supplier's delivery and the kiln start-up.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The process technology and vendor are fixed before design starts; vendor drawings for foundations arrive on the agreed dates; permanent power and water are available before cold commissioning; raw material for trial production is on site.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

rows: Presses, kiln, dryers & glazing lines (line supplier)

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy machines need crane access and often must enter before the cladding or a wall is closed. Vendor supervisors are booked for fixed periods. Clean, dry, powered conditions are required before precision equipment is unpacked.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: late supplier drawings or equipment, gas connection, press-pit and kiln-floor tolerances, and a long tuning period before quality is accepted. Contingency is held before first saleable production.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by plant area and discipline; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the installation crews and the vendor supervisors — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
